state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It's great that you're thinking about how the graph reflects Fido's movements. To clarify, the negative-sloping section represents Fido moving away from his home. Try to think about how distance and time are related in this scenario. Can you think of a way to determine Fido's movement during this part of the graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, but I'm confused - if the line is going down, doesn't that mean the distance is getting smaller? So wouldn't that mean Fido is getting closer to his home, not moving away from it? Or am I reading the graph wrong?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track in thinking about the relationship between the slope of the graph and Fido's movement. Remember, on a distance-time graph, a negative slope means that the distance is decreasing. So, in this case, the negative slope does indicate that Fido is getting closer to his home. Let's explore how we can interpret this in the context of the scenario.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher makes a critical error in Turn 1 by stating the negative slope represents moving away from home (contradicting the correct interpretation), then corrects this in Turn 3, but the student's improved understanding appears despite rather than because of the initial guidance.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher effectively scaffolds by breaking down the graph interpretation into manageable steps, adjusts support when the student shows confusion in Turn 2, and corrects their own error while validating the student's reasoning, though the initial incorrect statement in Turn 1 slightly undermines the overall quality.
